slides.title: Scale Factor: Perimeter and Area
slides.note: Post the learning target. Say one line and nothing else yet: “Today: the perimeter is multiplied by k too — and the area by k squared.”

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.sub: On your own. Four minutes. No notes.
slides.note: Q4 is the figure Notes I and II scale: 3 by 5, P = 16, A = 15. If perimeter and area are confused here, today has nothing to scale. Two minutes silent, then reveal.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Vocabulary
slides.sub: The new words, before they are used.
slides.note: Read each word and its meaning once; the notes use them next. Students copy the words, not the definitions.

slides.title: Notes
slides.sub: Copy the figure and the two lines.
slides.note: The 3 by 5 from the warm-up at k = 2: 6 by 10. Its perimeter was 16 and is 32 — doubled, because a perimeter is a sum of sides and every side doubled. Nobody has to recompute it. **Say:** the perimeter is made of lengths, so it is multiplied by the same k as the lengths.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note: Area is length × width, and both were multiplied by k, so the area is multiplied by k twice: 15 → 60, four times as much, not twice. The grid shows it: the copy holds four of the original. **Say:** area is two lengths multiplied, so k gets used twice — that is what k² means.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note: Run it backwards. Areas 20 and 180: 180 ÷ 20 = 9, and 9 is k², so k = √9 = 3. Then any side follows — a 4 cm side is 12 cm in the copy. Every area ratio in this unit is a perfect square. **Say:** the area ratio is k squared, so k is its square root.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: Ask which rule each part uses before anyone multiplies: perimeter × k, area × k².

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: P = 12 → 36 (× 3); A = 8 → 72 (× 9). A board with 24 for the area multiplied by k once — the guide's named misconception.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: P 18 → 72, A 18 → 288. Same structure, its own numbers (not the warm-up's 3 by 5). A board with 72 for the area multiplied by k once.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.sub: k from two areas, then a side.
slides.note: Ask what 180 ÷ 20 is, and whether that number is k.

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: 240 ÷ 15 = 16 is k², so k = 4, and the side is 12. A board with 48 took the area ratio as k. (Notes III's 20 → 180 is not reused.)

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: 300 ÷ 12 = 25, k = 5, the side is 10. A board with 50 took 25 as k.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 1 of 9
slides.note: Perimeter first. Nobody needs the sides: the perimeter is lengths, so × k.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 7 of 9
slides.note: The only non-rectangle (Math Nation 5.2.4's shape): the rule is about k, not about rectangles. The perimeter and the area are both 24 on purpose — the two answers show the two rules apart.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9
slides.note: The extra-number board (ruling 22): the 3 years is bait. Either route works — 10 by 15 is 150 too — and a board that found the sides first should say so.

slides.note: Written, and the exit evidence: the reason in a sentence with numbers. 'Because k²' alone names the rule and not the reason — ask for the two lengths.

slides.sub: Six questions. On your own, in writing.
slides.note: Hand out the Independent Set; the same six questions are on the board. Silent work. Circulate and mark what you see; do not teach. Whatever is not finished goes home.
